spots.name: Altmarkt
spots.label: Altmarkt

text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot. The centre of the square is then about 1 minute on foot to the east. The phone icon on the map is about 65 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description:
Altmarkt is the old market square in the heart of Dresden's Altstadt, and it is a handy first stop for a phone photographer. The open space gives you room to step back and fit a lot into the frame. That is rare in a historic centre, where streets are often too narrow for a wide view. The buildings around the square make a natural frame, and people crossing it give a sense of scale and everyday life.

The phone icon on the map is about 65 m west of the subject. From there you can take in the whole width of the square, with its edges leading the eye into the picture. Walk around a little before you settle. Small changes in position, or crouching a bit lower, change how much sky and paving you include.

Enjoy this square as a place to take in the old town's atmosphere rather than a single landmark. Take a general view first, then step closer for details such as building fronts and street scenes. Keep your phone lens clean, as a smudge shows up badly in bright, open scenes. If the square is busy or has temporary structures, the view may look different, so be ready to adjust your position.
text.geographic_location: Altmarkt is in the Innere Altstadt, the old town centre of Dresden, in the Altstadt district.
text.access_note: Altmarkt looks like an open public square, but check local event information before you go, as the square may be busy at times.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole square in, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for picking out details on the far side.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually has fewer people, if you want an emptier square. Evening light can be pleasant, and night mode helps once it gets dark.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 65 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. The square then opens out in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the middle of the scene to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so it keeps its colour. Try a Live Photo to catch people moving, and use panorama only if you want the whole width of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the horizon and building edges straight. Put the square's edge or a line of paving in the lower third to lead the eye across. Wait for people to walk through the frame to add scale. If you can, hold the phone at chest height rather than eye level for a steadier, cleaner view.

spots.name: Frauenkirche
spots.label: Frauenkirche

text.directions_text: Head for the Neumarkt square in the centre of Dresden. The phone icon on the map is about 90 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description:
The Frauenkirche (Church of Our Lady) is a Lutheran church in the middle of Dresden, and its bell-shaped dome gave the city a distinctive silhouette. The current building is the third church on this site. The Baroque church was built between 1726 and 1743 to a design by the city architect George Bähr. It was destroyed in the bombing of February 1945, and its ruins stood for nearly half a century as a war memorial. Rebuilding began in 1994, the exterior was finished in 2004 and the church was reconsecrated on 30 October 2005. The original dome, called the 'Stone Bell', was about 67 metres high and rested on eight slender supports. The surrounding Neumarkt square was rebuilt in 2004 with its Baroque-style buildings.

It photographs well because the curved dome and the pale, weathered stonework stand out against the surrounding buildings and the sky. From the phone icon on the map you are close enough to fill the frame with the church but still far enough back to see the dome and the lower walls together. Stand still for a moment before you shoot. Square-on shots work well, and so does a slight angle that shows the curves of the walls. People walking past the front add a sense of scale, so you don't need to wait for an empty frame.
text.geographic_location: The Frauenkirche stands in Dresden's old town, in the middle of the rebuilt Neumarkt square, with the Baroque-style buildings of the square around it.
text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the church itself is a place of worship and visitor site, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and any dress or entry rules.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the church and its dome together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the square and the buildings around it. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it for the dome and the stonework, but keep the phone still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light brings out the colour of the stone, and early in the day the square is usually quieter. After dark, night mode can work if you rest your elbows on something steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 90 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands and take a few frames in a row.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the centre of the dome with a vertical line so the church stands straight. Leave a little sky above the dome, and include some of the square in front for scale. Try one shot at 1x and one at 0.5x with the phone held level, so the walls don't lean.

spots.name: Zwinger
spots.label: Zwinger

text.directions_text: Make for the Innere Altstadt and Theaterplatz, next to the Semperoper; by taxi or hired scooter, ask for the Zwinger. The Elbe terraces are roughly 200 metres to the north-east, which helps you get your bearings. The phone icon on the map is about 75 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description: The Zwinger is a Baroque palace complex with gardens on the edge of Dresden's old town, designed by Matthäus Daniel Pöppelmann. It began in 1709 as an orangery, garden and festival ground for Augustus the Strong, and it is still one of the city's best-known buildings. Today it is a museum complex, home to the Old Masters Picture Gallery, the Porcelain Collection and the Mathematisch-Physikalischer Salon. It photographs well because the pavilions and long galleries are decorated with balustrades, statues and vases, so almost any angle gives you rhythm and detail. The name comes from a medieval word for the strip of ground between two defensive walls, even though the palace no longer served that purpose when it was built. Gottfried Semper closed the open side towards the Elbe with the Semper Gallery, which opened in 1855. Heavy bomb damage in February 1945 was followed by rebuilding in the 1950s and 1960s. Take one wide shot to show the scale, then move in for the carved figures, the gateways and the roofline. Look out for the Kronentor, the crown gate finished in 1714, which makes a good close-up of its own. Walk a few steps between shots, because the view changes quickly.
text.geographic_location: The Zwinger lies on the north-western edge of Dresden's Innere Altstadt (inner old town). It sits right beside Theaterplatz, the Semperoper and Dresden Castle.
text.access_note: The Zwinger is a museum and event complex, so access to the courtyard and the museums may vary; check the official site before you go.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the long galleries and pavilions into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of a single building. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for statues, vases and the Kronentor.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the stonework and fewer people in the frame. On a dull day the carved detail still shows well.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 75 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. From there the complex lies to the south-east, so you are looking across it rather than up at one wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest stone area to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the pale facades keep their detail. Leave Live Photos off unless people are moving through the scene, so you don't capture a blur.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the long gallery rooflines with the horizontal lines so they stay straight. Keep the phone level and avoid tilting it up, or the buildings will lean inwards. Use a pavilion or a row of statues as your main subject, and leave a little sky above it. Try one wide shot and one telephoto detail from the same spot.
